claims.text: High configurational mixing entropy in near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles suppresses atomic-diffusion-driven phase segregation at elevated temperatures.
Suppressing phase segregation preserves nanoparticle structural and chemical stability under catalytic and thermoelectric service conditions.
The initial nanoparticles are near-equiatomic, uniformly mixed solid solutions at room temperature.
A minor deviation from equiatomic elemental ratios lowers configurational entropy while elemental diversity remains constant.
Temperatures of 773–1173 K are representative of catalytic operation.
Temperatures of 473–1923 K are representative of thermoelectric operation.
Uniform elemental distribution without initial clustering or phase separation is characteristic of high-entropy systems.
High mixing entropy hinders atomic diffusion and redistribution.
Hindered atomic diffusion slows the kinetics of phase segregation under thermal stress.
A slight reduction in configurational entropy accelerates diffusion-driven segregation and causes structural changes.
Near-equiatomic nanoparticles will retain phase stability and a uniform microstructure longer than slightly off-equiatomic nanoparticles at high temperature.
Near-equiatomic, uniformly mixed nanoparticles typically maintain structural stability under service conditions.
The proposed entropy effect applies only to deviations small enough not to introduce additional destabilizing lattice-strain effects.
Extreme compositional deviations and samples containing secondary phases lie outside the proposed mechanistic regime.
Particle size and synthesis-procedure differences may influence thermal stability.

Failure of the reduced-entropy particles to exhibit a significantly higher segregation or instability rate under identical conditions would falsify the claim that mixing entropy is the primary stability mediator.
